title: Letting go
hookLine: the forest-dweller stage: Kunti leaves the palace for the forest, though her sons beg her to stay
tomorrow: Confucius waited at a village party. who was he waiting for?

lines: THE OLD KING LEAVES FOR THE FOREST.
HER SONS BEG HER TO STAY.
cards: Retirement parties have a strange mood: cake, speeches, and someone handing over the keys. The Mahabharata has a farewell with no cake. The war is over, the kingdom is safe, and the family is finally home.
Then the old blind king Dhritarashtra and his wife Gandhari decide to leave the palace and live in the forest. Kunti, mother of the brothers who won, goes with them. Her sons run after her.
Yudhishthira, king now, begs her to stay. Why, they ask, did you push us to fight for a kingdom you won't live in?

teach.b: Kunti's answer is clear. She urged them on for their sake, not hers. She had her share of royal life while her husband lived.
Now she wants to serve the old couple who are leaving, and give her days to prayer and austerity. And she walks on, with Gandhari's hand on her shoulder.
Gandhari keeps her eyes bound, as she has for years, so Kunti leads the way, and the old king follows.
This is the third Hindu stage, vanaprastha, the forest-dweller. The Laws of Manu name the moment: when a householder sees wrinkles, white hair and his children's children, he may go to the forest.
Not to run away, and not because life is over.
To hand the house to the next generation and turn toward what lasts. For some Hindu families today, the forest is a way of speaking.

It can look like handing over the business, the kitchen, the final word, and giving the time to prayer, pilgrimage and grandchildren. The hard part is the handing over. Kunti's sons wanted her to keep her place.

teach.h: LEAVE THE PLACE SO THEY CAN FILL IT.
teach.b: Her gift was to leave it, gladly, so they could fill it.
This stage asks for no less love, only love that makes room.

how: Hindu tradition names vanaprastha, the forest-dweller, as the third stage of life: the household passes to the next generation and an elder turns toward prayer and practice. Today some families live it as a way of stepping back rather than a move to the woods.

o: stepping back so the next generation can step in
quitting your job the moment you can afford it
moving somewhere quiet to escape your family

games.q: the walk to the forest: tap the pairs.
p: the mother who chose the forest
walked with her hand on Kunti's shoulder
the forest-dweller stage, third of four

s: in Hindu teaching, the forest stage means running away from family
it means handing the household to the next generation and turning toward practice.
Kunti's sons begged her to stay in the palace
she went anyway, to serve the old king and queen and to give her days to austerity.
the Laws of Manu link the forest stage to signs like white hair and grandchildren
when a householder sees wrinkles, white hair and his children's children, he may go to the forest.

games.q: your aunt runs every family holiday and is worn out, but says if she lets go, it'll all fall apart. what would the forest-dweller stage say?
o: hand it on to the next ones and step back gladly; that's the gift of the stage.
never let go: in Hindu teaching, elders must keep control to the end.
stop hosting with no warning; stepping back means cutting people off.
games.why: in vanaprastha the household passes to the next generation. Kunti left her place so her sons could fill it.

practice: Choose one thing you could give away: a book you've finished, a jacket, a tool, a job you've held too long. Set it by the door, or name the person who should have it.
Then sit for the rest of the time with empty hands in your lap, and notice whether letting go feels light or heavy.

wordCard.voice: Letting go: vanaprastha, the forest-dweller stage, third of the four. Handing the house to the next ones, and turning toward what lasts.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the forest-dweller; the third of the four stages of life.

carryVoice: Carry this: stepping back, the way Kunti walked to the forest, gladly, so her sons could step in. Day 1685, keys handed over.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Ashramavasika Parva (Dhritarashtra and Gandhari leave for the forest; Kunti goes with them; her sons beg her to stay; she answers that she urged them to fight for their sake, had her share of royal life, and now chooses to serve her elders and practice austerity)
Laws of Manu 6.2-3 (when a householder sees his skin wrinkled, his hair white, and the sons of his sons, he may go to the forest)
